title: Two Places the Adult Brain Still Makes Neurons

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: A thymidine birth label enters newly copied DNA during {{c1::S phase}} of the cell cycle.
cards.quote: A cell copies its DNA once per division, in S phase,
cards.section: How you know a neuron is new

cards.front: What two kinds of evidence must coincide in an adult brain cell to identify it as an adult-born neuron?
cards.back: A birth record of DNA copying during adulthood and neuronal identity in the same cell, with controls for DNA repair and abortive DNA synthesis.
cards.quote: A neuron counts as new only when the same cells carry two facts at once: a birth record,
cards.section: How you know a neuron is new

cards.front: Why can BrdU and NeuN staining together resolve the identity problem of a DNA-labelled cell beside a neuron?
cards.back: Antibodies detect BrdU in newly copied DNA and NeuN as neuronal identity. Finding both in the same cell avoids assigning a neighbouring glial label to a neuron.
cards.quote: so the same cell can be stained for BrdU and for a neuron-only protein such as NeuN.
cards.section: How you know a neuron is new

cards.front: Why does a thymidine pulse not give the exact last-division date of a labelled neuron found weeks later?
cards.back: Its precursor may divide again after the pulse. The label dates DNA copying in that lineage; the neuron’s last division may occur that day or later.
cards.quote: A labelled precursor can divide again after the label has cleared,
cards.section: How you know a neuron is new

cards.front: An adult neuron incorporates a DNA label, but controls show incorporation through DNA repair. What happens to the claim that this is a newborn neuron, and why?
cards.back: The label no longer supports a new birth: repair can incorporate it without cell division. Neuronal identity alone does not restore the missing birth record.
cards.quote: Label can also enter a cell that never divided: through DNA repair,
cards.section: How you know a neuron is new

cards.front: In an adult canary, a DNA pulse label appears first at the ventricle and weeks later in HVC cells confirmed as neurons by electron microscopy. What process does this support?
cards.back: Birth at the ventricle followed by migration into HVC. The label provides the birth record, microscopy establishes neuronal identity, and the time sequence supports migration.
cards.quote: So the new neurons were born at the ventricle and migrated in
cards.section: How you know a neuron is new

cards.front: Name the two well-established neurogenic niches in adult rodents and locate each.
cards.back: The subventricular zone (SVZ), in the lateral ventricle wall; and the subgranular zone (SGZ), at the inner edge of the dentate gyrus.
cards.quote: The second is the subgranular zone (SGZ) at the inner edge of the dentate gyrus,
cards.section: Two places adult rodents keep making neurons

cards.front: In adult rodents, SVZ neuroblasts reach the olfactory bulb along the {{c1::rostral migratory stream}}.
cards.back: They migrate in chains and become local interneurons.
cards.quote: line up in chains and travel forward along the rostral migratory stream to the olfactory bulb,
cards.section: Two places adult rodents keep making neurons

cards.front: Matched groups of young adult and middle-aged rats are tested for dentate gyrus neurogenesis. What age-related difference is expected, and why?
cards.back: The middle-aged group should show much less neurogenesis: the rat dentate gyrus rate has already fallen sharply by middle age. Continued production does not imply a constant rate.
cards.quote: In the dentate gyrus the rate falls steeply with age:
cards.section: Two places adult rodents keep making neurons

cards.front: What two abilities define the astrocyte-like stem cells in the adult rodent SVZ and dentate gyrus?
cards.back: Each can divide to make more of itself and produce cells that become neurons.
cards.quote: A stem cell here means a cell that can divide to make more of itself and also make cells that become neurons.
cards.section: Which cell is the stem cell?

cards.front: Trace the adult rodent SVZ lineage from the astrocyte-like stem cell to its neuronal product.
cards.back: B cell (astrocyte-like stem cell) → C cell (fast-dividing precursor) → A cell (migrating neuroblast) → olfactory bulb interneuron.
cards.quote: B cell (astrocyte-like stem cell) → C cell (fast-dividing, transit-amplifying precursor) → A cell (neuroblast) → olfactory bulb interneuron
cards.section: Which cell is the stem cell?

cards.front: How do transit-amplifying C cells increase neuron output from rarely dividing adult rodent SVZ stem cells?
cards.back: C cells divide quickly a few times, multiplying the precursor population before it produces neuroblasts.
cards.quote: divide quickly a few times, multiplying the number of cells on the way to neurons.
cards.section: Which cell is the stem cell?

cards.front: An adult mouse SVZ receives a drug that kills cells copying DNA. What happens to fast-dividing C cells versus rarely dividing B and ependymal cells, and why?
cards.back: C cells are depleted; B and ependymal cells tend to survive. Many C cells enter DNA synthesis during treatment, whereas the rarely dividing populations are less exposed to the drug’s killing condition.
cards.quote: The cells that divide rarely, the ependymal cells and the astrocyte-like B cells, survived.
cards.section: Which cell is the stem cell?

cards.front: In untreated adult mice, a retrovirus infects only dividing GFAP-expressing astrocyte-like cells. Its inherited marker later appears in olfactory bulb neurons. What does this establish?
cards.back: Those neurons descend from astrocyte-like cells and were born after infection. The inherited marker supplies ancestry and a division record; identifying the descendants as neurons supplies neuronal identity.
cards.quote: The neurons had descended from astrocyte-like cells, and were born after the infection; the ancestry was the new information.
cards.section: Which cell is the stem cell?

cards.front: After an antimitotic drug, adult mouse SVZ B cells regenerate C cells and neuroblasts. How would you test whether B cells also normally make neurons, rather than only repairing drug damage?
cards.back: Trace an inherited label from astrocyte-like B cells to identified neurons in untreated mice. The birth-record-and-identity rule, extended by ancestry tracing, tests normal neuron production without relying on recovery from injury.
cards.quote: a cell that survives a poison and divides afterwards might be repairing the zone, not running it.
cards.section: Which cell is the stem cell?

cards.front: What different steps do early BrdU counts and later BrdU-plus-NeuN counts measure in adult rodent dentate gyrus?
cards.back: At one day, BrdU counts index precursor division. Weeks later, BrdU-plus-NeuN counts identify labelled cells that became neurons and were kept.
cards.quote: Weeks later, cells carrying both BrdU and NeuN are the labelled cells that became neurons and were kept.
cards.section: Born is not the same as kept

cards.front: Why is late BrdU-plus-NeuN count divided by early BrdU count a neuron yield rather than a pure survival rate?
cards.back: Labelled precursors may divide again, and some daughters become glia. The ratio therefore combines later division, neuronal fate and survival.
cards.quote: It is not quite a survival rate, because labelled precursors can divide again after the first day and some daughters become glia;
cards.section: Born is not the same as kept

cards.front: Toy adult-mouse dentate data: controls and treated mice each have 1,000 BrdU cells at one day. At four weeks, BrdU-plus-NeuN counts are 500 and 1,000, respectively. Calculate neuron yield in each group and interpret the difference.
cards.back: Control yield = 500/1,000 = 0.5 neuron per early labelled cell; treated yield = 1,000/1,000 = 1.0. Treatment doubles yield without changing the early division index.
cards.why: This does not isolate survival: later precursor division and neuronal fate can also change yield.
cards.quote: Dividing the late count by the early count gives a neuron yield per early labelled cell.
cards.section: Born is not the same as kept

cards.front: Suppose enriched housing improves only survival of young dentate neurons in adult mice. What happens to early BrdU counts, later BrdU-plus-NeuN counts and their ratio, and why?
cards.back: Early counts stay the same; later neuron counts and neuron yield rise. Keeping more offspring increases the late count without increasing the initial division index. Assume later division and fate choice are unchanged.
cards.quote: Enriched housing acted mainly on survival: mice housed in larger cages with toys and companions had more surviving new neurons
cards.section: Born is not the same as kept

cards.front: What does poorer survival of young dentate neurons lacking NMDA receptors in mice suggest about which newborn neurons are kept?
cards.back: Survival during maturation depends partly on the young neuron’s own activity. It does not establish a target-derived factor such as NGF as the mechanism.
cards.why: In mice, many newborn cells die within days of birth. The activity-dependent survival effect occurs later, while young neurons mature.
cards.quote: young dentate neurons lacking NMDA receptors, a type of glutamate receptor, survived less well than their neighbours
cards.section: Born is not the same as kept

cards.front: How do Notch and Wnt differ in their stated roles in adult neurogenic niches?
cards.back: Notch helps reserve resting stem cells, although some Notch signals also sustain dividing stem cells. Wnt pushes precursors toward neurons.
cards.quote: Notch signalling helps keep stem cells at rest, in reserve
cards.section: Born is not the same as kept

cards.front: Wnt signalling is blocked in an adult rat neurogenic niche. What happens to neuron production, and why?
cards.back: Neuron production should fall strongly; blocking Wnt nearly abolished it in adult rats. Wnt normally pushes precursors toward neuronal production.
cards.quote: in adult rats extra Wnt3 increased neuron production, while blocking Wnt signalling nearly abolished it
cards.section: Born is not the same as kept

cards.front: The dentate gyrus process of giving similar places or events distinct representations is {{c1::pattern separation}}.
cards.quote: That job is pattern separation, telling apart similar places or events.
cards.section: New neurons join working circuits

cards.front: Why might young adult-born dentate granule neurons contribute to pattern separation in rodents?
cards.back: While maturing, they fire more readily to weak input. A leading hypothesis is that this excitable population helps turn similar inputs into different outputs.
cards.quote: A leading hypothesis is that a small, excitable young population helps the dentate gyrus give two similar inputs different outputs.
cards.section: New neurons join working circuits

cards.front: Some adult-born canary HVC neurons respond to sound during recordings. What does this add beyond evidence that they were newly born neurons?
cards.back: It supports functional participation in a circuit. A birth record plus neuronal identity establishes new neurons; sound-evoked activity addresses whether those neurons function in an existing circuit.
cards.quote: recorded from new neurons in the canary song nucleus HVC and found that some of them responded to sound.
cards.section: New neurons join working circuits

cards.front: In rodents, the supply of adult-born olfactory bulb interneurons has been linked to {{c1::odour learning}}.
cards.quote: In the rodent olfactory bulb, the steady supply of new interneurons has been linked to odour learning.
cards.section: New neurons join working circuits

cards.front: Runners outperform sedentary mice at distinguishing nearby locations. Design a test of whether adult-born dentate neurons are needed for the advantage while excluding a general performance deficit.
cards.back: Block adult neurogenesis in runners and test whether the nearby-location advantage disappears. Check running, other-cell damage and far-apart discrimination. The necessity rule requires perturbation plus controls showing that the loss is specific.
cards.quote: Check that the block does not stop the mice running, harm other cells, or impair the easy far-apart task;
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Running improves mouse location discrimination and increases late BrdU-plus-NeuN counts. Which additional birth-label measurements would distinguish increased initial division from increased later neuron yield?
cards.back: Measure one-day BrdU counts and compare late/early yield between runners and controls. By the two-time-point rule, an early increase with unchanged yield supports increased initial division; higher yield requires further measurements of later division, fate and death.
cards.quote: Count BrdU cells one day after the dose too, so you can see whether running changed the early count, the later neuron yield, or both.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What did BrdU-plus-NeuN cells in the adult dentate gyrus of cancer patients support, and what population-level inference remained limited?
cards.back: They supported adult-born human neurons: adult DNA labelling and neuronal identity coincided. They did not establish a birth rate or the same rate in healthy people.
cards.quote: Those cells most likely descended from cells that copied their DNA while the patients were adults, and were neurons when they died.
cards.section: New neurons in the adult human brain

cards.front: Why can atmospheric carbon-14 act as a birth record in neuronal DNA?
cards.back: Atmospheric carbon enters DNA when cells divide. Neurons normally stop copying their genome after their last division, preserving a record of DNA synthesis.
cards.quote: the DNA of a cell that never divides again keeps the carbon-14 of its birth year.
cards.section: Carbon-14: a birth record everyone carries

cards.front: In human carbon-14 studies, which two neuronal populations had DNA matching the person’s birth-year atmosphere?
cards.back: Neurons at the back of the cerebral cortex and in the olfactory bulb.
cards.quote: the DNA of neurons at the back of the cerebral cortex matches the air of the person's own birth year,
cards.section: Carbon-14: a birth record everyone carries

cards.front: An adult human hippocampal neuronal DNA sample differs from the birth-year carbon-14 expectation beyond error and normal early development. What does it support, and which alternative carbon sources require controls?
cards.back: It supports addition of some neurons after birth. Controls must rule out DNA repair, extra DNA copies and stray non-neuronal nuclei as explanations for the mismatch. The pooled reading alone does not specify how many neurons were added or when.
cards.quote: unless DNA repair, cells with extra copies of their DNA or stray non-neuronal nuclei in the sorted sample add carbon.
cards.section: Carbon-14: a birth record everyone carries

cards.front: A donor born in 1972 has pooled hippocampal neuronal carbon-14 matching air from 1976. Why can this not uniquely establish a neuronal birth year or daily birth rate?
cards.back: The mixture rule averages carbon-14 across nuclei. All DNA made in 1976 and mixtures of birth-year and later DNA can share a reading; carbon-14 is not averaged calendar years. A rate additionally needs a turnover model.
cards.quote: The reading alone cannot tell which, and because the sample averages carbon-14, not years, 1976 is not simply the mean birth year either.
cards.section: Carbon-14: a birth record everyone carries

cards.front: DCX staining is intended to indicate an immature {{c1::state}}, rather than a date of birth.
cards.quote: If the adult human dentate gyrus holds cells that are immature in their markers but were born long ago,
cards.section: Markers: a state, not a birth date

cards.front: Toy model for one human hippocampus: suppose about 700 neurons/day enter a DCX-positive state, all survive and stay positive for 21 days, and entry is steady. Estimate the simultaneous DCX-positive count.
cards.back: Count = entry rate × duration = 700 neurons/day × 21 days = 14,700 DCX-positive neurons, about 15,000 in one hippocampus.
cards.why: The lesson’s 700/day is a model average of neurons that persisted, not measured DCX entry. Human DCX duration is unknown, so this is conditional arithmetic.
cards.quote: the number marked at any moment is the rate times that time.
cards.section: Markers: a state, not a birth date

cards.front: Matched blocks from one adult human hippocampus lose DCX staining as fixation is prolonged. What does this show about interpreting an adult sample with no DCX-positive cells?
cards.back: A negative stain can reflect tissue handling rather than absence of young neurons. Fixation can weaken the detectable antigen; matched blocks isolate a handling effect more directly than comparisons between different donors.
cards.quote: DCX staining weakens with time after death and with long fixation, so a negative result may mean the antigen was lost.
cards.section: Markers: a state, not a birth date

cards.front: One human hippocampal study counts many DCX-positive cells, while another uses carbon-14 to infer some later-born neurons. Why need these methods not count the same population?
cards.back: Apply the state-versus-birth rule: some DCX-positive cells may have been born long ago, and carbon-14 averages DNA birth records. Their agreement or disagreement alone cannot establish a common population or human function.
cards.quote: a marker count and a carbon-14 estimate could both be correct and still describe different things.
cards.section: Markers: a state, not a birth date

cards.front: How certain are adult human hippocampal neurogenesis and its functional role compared with the rodent evidence?
cards.back: Birth-record methods favour some human hippocampal neurogenesis, but its rate, variation and function remain unsettled. Rodent circuit and behavioural roles do not transfer automatically to people.
cards.quote: In people, the evidence that carries a birth record points to some hippocampal neurogenesis.
cards.section: Putting it together

cards.front: Compare carbon-14 evidence in donors born before the bomb rise and on the falling curve. Why is increased hippocampal DNA carbon-14 in a pre-bomb donor a cleaner timing test than a small decrease in the later donor?
cards.back: Combine DNA dating with curve shape: the flat pre-bomb baseline makes later bomb-carbon incorporation clearer and reduces the impact of timing errors. On the steep falling curve, small timing or dietary-lag errors can rival a small signal. Repair, extra-DNA and sorting controls still apply.
cards.quote: Before the bomb the curve is nearly flat, and those errors matter much less.
cards.section: Two donors on the curve

cards.front: What assumptions condition the estimate of about 700 new neurons per human hippocampus per day from carbon-14 data?
cards.back: It depends on the chosen turnover model, pure neuronal sorting and little carbon added by DNA repair. It is a model estimate, not a direct daily count.
cards.quote: The estimate rests on the model chosen, on pure neuronal sorting, and on DNA repair adding little carbon.
cards.section: The hippocampal turnover estimate
